input.quote: Expressed in corneal luminance, the cat detected gratings at luminances 0.74 log units lower than the human observers did.
Expressed in retinal illuminance, after correcting for the larger pupil and ocular transmission, the cat's scotopic threshold was -0.08 log units re human.

content.thinking: Both passages found; explain corneal vs retinal.

content.text:
Here is where it comes from. The library value is behavioural, scotopic, at low spatial frequencies, in the domestic cat (Felis catus). In the Results the paper says: “Expressed in corneal luminance, the cat detected gratings at luminances 0.74 log units lower than the human observers did.”

That number includes the cat's optics, mainly its much larger pupil. The same section goes on: “Expressed in retinal illuminance, after correcting for the larger pupil and ocular transmission, the cat's scotopic threshold was -0.08 log units re human.” The library's own note says the same thing: most of the advantage is optics, and with optics factored out cat and human scotopic sensitivity are similar.

For a robot camera this matters. The camera has its own lens and aperture, so the cat's pupil does not come with it. If you want the profile to model the retina rather than the eye's optics, the optics-removed value is the closer match. That is your call as the biologist.

content.thinking: The person decided: use the optics-removed value. Propose a claim revision with the verified quote.

content.text: I'll propose that change. You'll see a card with Approve and Reject; nothing changes until you approve it.

changes.conditions: Behavioural, scotopic, low spatial frequencies; expressed in retinal illuminance (pupil and ocular transmission factored out).
changes.quote: Expressed in retinal illuminance, after correcting for the larger pupil and ocular transmission, the cat's scotopic threshold was -0.08 log units re human.

input.reason: For a robot camera the lens, not the cat's pupil, sets how much light reaches the sensor, so the optics-removed threshold is the one to use.

content.text: I'll work out what the new value does to Panther's profiles.

Four profile values read this number: the camera-frame gain table and the event-camera attention, in both panther and panther_vision. With the optics-removed value, Panther trusts the camera image only in brighter light and hands over to the event camera sooner as it gets dark. The world model does not read this value yet, so the world prior is unchanged; I've noted that gap as an open question. The reflex threshold does not change.
I'll run the bench on those two recordings against the unchanged baseline. This takes a few minutes.

The results are in, from the stored experiment record. On the two recordings there were 24 labelled objects per arm, enough to judge.

- panther_prior: hit rate 50% before and 67% with the new value. But the chance hit rate, the luck check, also rose, from 49% to 64%. So most of that gain is what the same amount of firing would get by luck; this does not show that the new value makes Panther better at noticing objects.
- null_profile (the control, no priors): hit rate 42% before and after, chance 42%.
- Median delay stayed at 0.30 s for panther_prior, false fires stayed at 120 per hour, and p99 latency at 2.0 ms.

In short, the bench shows no clear benefit or harm on these two recordings. Whether to change the library is a question about the biology, which you have already answered.
I'll propose the library change with that experiment attached. You'll see a card; approving it opens a pull request on profiles for review.

input.rationale: For a robot camera the lens replaces the cat's pupil, so the library should carry the optics-removed scotopic threshold (-0.08 log10 re human, Kang et al. 2009, Results).
